data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy": null, "claim": "Popper's preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on his own terms not as an inductive inference that the theory is more likely true, but as a critical rationalist rule of action: we act on the theory that has withstood the most severe tests because it offers the best available (though fallible) grasp of reality, while explicitly rejecting the notion that this survival increases its logical probability. The cost of accepting this view is the abandonment of 'probabilistic security'—the comfort of believing our actions are backed by high statistical likelihood—and the acceptance that all scientific action remains a bold conjecture, even when based on extensive corroboration.", "counterconditions": [{"case": "If corroboration is shown to logically entail a higher probability of future success, the distinction collapses into induction.", "checker_spec": null, "eval": "observation"}, {"case": "If Popper's own writings imply he relied on an implicit inductive principle when choosing theories for practical application.", "checker_spec": null, "eval": "observation"}, {"case": "If the concept of 'verisimilitude' (truth-likeness), often used to bridge this gap, is proven formally incoherent within Popper's framework, leaving no metric for 'better' theories other than survival.", "checker_spec": null, "eval": "observation"}], "definitions": [], "derivation": [], "formalization_refs": [], "mechanism": "The argument distinguishes between 'logical probability' (which Popper rejects as increased by testing) and 'rational preferability for action' (which he accepts). It posits that corroboration reports past performance under severe tests, serving as a critical filter rather than an inductive booster. The preference is justified pragmatically and critically: since we must act, and since falsified theories are known to be false while corroborated ones are merely not-yet-falsified, the latter are the only rational candidates for action. This avoids induction by refusing to claim the future will resemble the past; it simply states that among current options, the unrefuted one is the only non-irrational choice.", "premises": [], "schema": "deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1", "scope": {"covers": [], "excludes": ["Popper's preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on his own terms not as an inductive inference that the theory is more likely true, but as a critical rationalist rule of action: we"]}, "simulation_refs": [], "uncertainties": []}
